title: Glenohumeral Osteoarthritis
case: Case: A 66-year-old retired builder has 2 years of slowly worsening right shoulder pain and stiffness, with grinding when he lifts the arm. He had a dislocation 20 years ago. Passive external rotation is greatly reduced with crepitus. X-ray shows joint space narrowing and osteophytes.

Working diagnosis: glenohumeral osteoarthritis, probably secondary to previous dislocation. Plan: education, gentle range work, cuff and scapular strengthening, pain advice, review for injection or surgical discussion if function remains poor.
qa: How do you separate GH OA from frozen shoulder? Both limit passive external rotation. X-ray shows joint changes in OA and is usually normal in frozen shoulder, and the clinical course differs.
Why not promise that exercise will rebuild the joint? There is no evidence that it reverses the joint changes. The aim is better pain, function and confidence.
Why is a severe sudden pain in a steroid-treated patient urgent? It may be a fracture or avascular necrosis and needs imaging.
The patient fears the X-ray means surgery. What do you say? Many people with X-ray changes manage with non-surgical care, and surgery is considered when symptoms are severe and persistent.
Why check passive range, not only active? It shows whether the limit comes from the joint itself.

fields.Action: Place a hand over the front or back of the joint and move the arm passively through rotation or elevation
fields.Positive: Palpable grinding or crepitus with familiar pain
fields.Supports: Joint surface involvement, not a specific diagnosis

redFlags.Finding: Sudden severe pain after minimal trauma in an older or steroid-treated patient
Rapid deterioration over weeks, severe night pain
Weight loss, cancer history, constant pain
Multiple swollen painful joints with morning stiffness

manual.name: Low-grade glenohumeral mobilization
manual.application: Supine, gentle oscillations in pain-free range

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: education and exercise. Manual therapy is optional for short-term comfort. Do not claim that mobilization rebuilds cartilage or reverses the arthritis. Avoid forceful end-range stretching because it can increase pain [Ref - to verify].

exercise.Steps: Table slide, wall walk, stick-assisted raise
Lying, push the hand outward with the other arm

exerciseNotes: Exercise has not been shown to reverse the joint changes, but it may improve pain and function [Ref - to verify]. Pain up to about 3 to 4 out of 10 that settles within a day is a common guide. Weight management and general health advice may help, especially when there are other joints involved.
modalityNotes: Medical options: pain medication, intra-articular corticosteroid injection (short-term relief for some), and joint replacement (anatomic or reverse, depending on the cuff and bone) for severe, persistent cases [Ref - to verify]. These are doctor decisions. Rehabilitation after surgery follows the surgeon's protocol.
pathway: Any emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.
Older age or past injury, gradual pain, reduced passive external rotation with crepitus? Yes: working diagnosis is probable GH OA; ask for an X-ray to confirm and separate from frozen shoulder.
Mild to moderate symptoms? Yes: start conservative care.
Severe pain, major loss of function, or no improvement after reasonable non-surgical care? Yes: discuss specialist review, injection or joint replacement [Ref - to verify].
Visit 1: screen flags, examine, request or review imaging through a doctor, explain OA in plain terms.
Early: reduce painful loading, gentle movement, optional low-grade mobilization.
Middle: strengthen the cuff and scapular muscles, build function and fitness.
Late: self-management plan for flares, activity pacing, adaptive tools.
